title: Hey, Baby, Whats Wrong? (1)

jokes.text: Criss's Valentine's song with placeholder chorus: '# and the chorus goes here / yeah this is where the chorus goes #' and '# I didn't have time to write it / but the chorus goes here #'
jokes.setup: Criss is serenading Liz with a heartfelt Valentine's Day song, building romantic expectation
jokes.punchline: The chorus is literally the words 'this is where the chorus goes' — he didn't finish writing it
jokes.explanation: Perfectly structured absurdist joke. The setup builds romantic expectation, then the punchline is that the chorus is literally a placeholder — and he keeps singing it earnestly. The joke escalates as he commits to it. It's character-specific (Criss is lovably feckless) and the structure mirrors Liz's complaint later that he 'wings everything.' Genuinely original comedic concept executed with perfect economy.

jokes.text: Liz says she prefers to celebrate 'the 1920 founding of the League of Women Voters in Chicago, Illinois. Interesting fact: They were supposed to meet on the 13th, but they all got lost, so...'
jokes.setup: Criss says 'But you're a lady' implying she should love Valentine's Day
jokes.punchline: Liz pivots to a hyper-specific feminist historical fact, then undercuts women with a joke about getting lost — self-deprecating in the most Liz Lemon way possible
jokes.explanation: Classic Liz Lemon joke — she deflects romance with an overly specific factoid, then accidentally undercuts the feminist point with a sexist stereotype delivered as throwaway. The trailing 'so...' is perfect economy. Deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: Criss proposes dinner at home with 'mashed potatoes in a Martini glass, we'll open some of that wine we didn't give the super for Christmas because you decided it would come off as racist. Oh, I'm glad we gave him those G.E.D. books instead.'
jokes.setup: Criss tries to make a romantic home dinner sound appealing
jokes.punchline: The wine callback reveals they gave the super GED books as a Christmas gift — equally (if not more) condescending than wine
jokes.explanation: Two-part joke that rewards attention. 'Wine would be racist' sets up liberal guilt, then the punchline that GED books is somehow the better choice is a perfect escalation of clueless wokeness. Very character-specific for both Liz and Criss's dynamic.

jokes.text: 'We'll play the soundtrack to Major League.' / 'You're making fun of me, but that love song is awesome.'
jokes.setup: Criss lists romantic dinner elements — candles, real silverware — building toward something beautiful
jokes.punchline: The Major League soundtrack as romantic dinner music, and his earnest defense of it
jokes.explanation: Quick absurdist character joke. The escalation from 'real silverware' and 'candles' to 'Major League soundtrack' is a funny anti-climax, and Criss doubling down is perfect. Economy is the strength here.

jokes.text: Liz says she is '0 for 40 on Valentine's Day.' Cut to: 'I will waste you! You'll have to go through this old bastard first! Bon Jovi.'
jokes.setup: Liz declares she is 0 for 40 on Valentine's Day, implying a montage of bad experiences
jokes.punchline: A cutaway to Bon Jovi blocking Liz from a Valentine, delivered as an absurd historical aside
jokes.explanation: Perfectly executed 30 Rock cutaway gag. The specificity of Bon Jovi as a Valentine's nemesis is wonderfully absurd. 'You'll have to go through this old bastard first!' followed by simply 'Bon Jovi.' as the reveal is beautifully economical. High quotability.

jokes.text: Jack approaches Liz and uses his dead mother as a Valentine's pitch: 'you know, my mom did just die. Will you be my Valentine?'
jokes.setup: Jack tries to stop Liz from leaving, saying 'No, no, no, no, no, Lemon'
jokes.punchline: He uses his mother's fresh death as a manipulation tactic to get Liz to be his Valentine — a darkly comic non sequitur
jokes.explanation: Jack's willingness to weaponize grief for social leverage is pitch-perfect character comedy. The deadpan delivery — pivoting from 'my mom just died' to 'will you be my Valentine' — is very Jack Donaghy.

jokes.text: Tracy's response to Jack's Valentine pitch: 'I just realized I'm gay.'
jokes.setup: Jack has made an awkward Valentine's pitch; the scene needs a comic button
jokes.punchline: Tracy's non-sequitur announcement that he's just realized he's gay as a way of declining/escaping
jokes.explanation: Classic Tracy non-sequitur button joke. Pure economy — four words that land a laugh. Not deeply crafted but perfectly deployed.

jokes.text: Jack explains his extra energy from Avery's absence: 'My animus has become pent up.' Tracy: 'Why don't you just come out and say you haven't had mommy-daddy sheet monster times.' Jack: 'I'm not about to cheat on the woman I love, and I've never mommy-daddy sheet monstered myself.'
jokes.setup: Jack diplomatically describes being sexually frustrated using euphemisms
jokes.punchline: Tracy's blunt invented phrase 'mommy-daddy sheet monster times' replaces all Jack's dignity; Jack's denial that he's never masturbated is the button
jokes.explanation: Tracy's invented euphemism 'mommy-daddy sheet monster times' is inspired wordplay — childlike and yet perfectly explicit. Jack's prim denial of ever masturbating is peak Jack Donaghy character comedy. The contrast between Jack's 'animus has become pent up' and Tracy's blunt invention generates the laugh. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: 'Never? Not even during the Love Boat reunion?'
jokes.setup: Jack claims he's never masturbated
jokes.punchline: Tracy's very specific cultural reference — the Love Boat reunion — as the ultimate irresistible masturbation occasion
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the previous joke. The specificity of 'the Love Boat reunion' — implying it was so sexy it should have broken anyone's resolve — is absurdist and oddly specific in exactly the right 30 Rock way. Extremely economical.

jokes.text: Jack's Valentine's Day flashback: 'We're not going to Chili's until I hit one.' Golf ball hits him in the crotch. 'I would kill to get hit in the crotch by a baseball today.'
jokes.setup: Jack says he knows what it's like to have a crummy Valentine's Day, implying past romantic disappointments
jokes.punchline: The flashback reveals his Valentine's frustration was about golf, and he took a ball to the crotch; his present self wishes for that simpler problem
jokes.explanation: Decent visual/physical gag with an ironic twist — the crotch shot is now desirable compared to his current situation. Competent but not particularly original.

jokes.text: Jack explaining his mother-in-law situation: 'The first Jessup moved to this country in 1760 to avoid an embarrassing regifting incident.'
jokes.setup: Jack explains the Jessups are very white and very proper
jokes.punchline: Their entire immigration to America was motivated by a regifting faux pas — a delightfully tiny, WASP-specific motivation for a historic event
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy joke. Compressing the entire Jessup family's immigration narrative into a regifting scandal is a perfect piece of WASP satire. The historical grandeur (1760, immigration to America) vs. the absurdly trivial reason (regifting) is a beautifully constructed incongruity. The joke does enormous world-building in one sentence. Justifies the 8.0.

jokes.text: Pete on mother-in-laws: 'I've never had a mother-in-law, but I have seen Everybody Loves Raymond' — then launches into spot-on impression of Raymond's mother dynamic
jokes.setup: Jack laments his incoming mother-in-law
jokes.punchline: Pete's only frame of reference is Everybody Loves Raymond, which he reenacts verbatim including 'Ma!'
jokes.explanation: The meta-TV joke lands well — using a rival network's show as the cultural reference point for mother-in-law dynamics is funny. The 'Ma!' callback is a nice button.

jokes.text: Jack's 'denial' pun: 'What is she, an Egyptian crocodile? 'Cause she is in denial.' Then: 'I've had two coffees.'
jokes.setup: Jack explains Diana won't acknowledge the reality of Avery's kidnapping situation
jokes.punchline: He makes a 'Nile/denial' pun, then immediately undercuts it himself with 'I've had two coffees' as explanation for the terrible joke
jokes.explanation: The meta-self-awareness of Jack immediately explaining away his own bad pun ('I've had two coffees') is the real joke — it's not really about the pun but about Jack's embarrassment at having made it. Deeply character-specific: Jack Donaghy does not make puns, so he has to rationalize it.

jokes.text: Elevator scene: Jack is telling Tracy his plan to give Valentine's a second chance, then the elevator opens and cuts the conversation off with 'What a shame. It felt like we were just getting started.' / '"Ma!"'
jokes.setup: Jack is making a heartfelt declaration about Valentine's Day
jokes.punchline: The elevator door opens, cutting him off perfectly, and Tracy's 'Ma!' Everybody Loves Raymond callback lands as the button
jokes.explanation: Functional structural joke — the elevator door as comedic punctuation. The running 'Ma!' gag is well-timed if slightly thin on its own.

jokes.text: Hazel orientation speech: 'Valentine's Day is a celebration of the burning of a Catholic loudmouth, but it's also about love. And escort prices going way up.'
jokes.setup: Hazel is giving new-page orientation on Valentine's Day
jokes.punchline: She casually mentions escort price surges as a Valentine's Day factoid, delivered with the same weight as the historical note
jokes.explanation: Good economy joke — the pairing of 'burning of a Catholic loudmouth' with 'escort prices going way up' creates comedic escalation through unexpected juxtaposition. The deadpan delivery of the escort line as a throwaway is what makes it work.

jokes.text: Hazel's backstory: 'I managed a haunted house upstate. But, as you know, the haunted house industry is a real boys' club.'
jokes.setup: Hazel talks about her career background before becoming a page
jokes.punchline: She applies serious feminist critique ('real boys' club') to the haunted house industry, treating it as a legitimate career sector with glass ceilings
jokes.explanation: A very 30 Rock joke — applying real-world workplace gender dynamics to an utterly absurd industry. The straight-faced delivery of 'the haunted house industry is a real boys' club' is what elevates it.

jokes.text: Jenna uses Hazel to test 'unapproved Japanese medications.' 'Swallow. Good girl. Now let me know if all your pubic hair falls out.' / 'Oh, my God!' / 'Oh, no, that's what it's supposed to do. I want to make sure it doesn't cause seizures.'
jokes.setup: Jenna welcomes Hazel as the only female page and says how great it is
jokes.punchline: She immediately uses Hazel as a human test subject for unapproved drugs, with escalating details (pubic hair, then seizures) that keep topping themselves
jokes.explanation: Classic Jenna Maroney joke — her narcissism and cruelty are expressed through the veneer of sisterhood. The escalation from 'so great to have a woman page here' to 'swallow' to 'let me know if your pubic hair falls out' to 'I want to make sure it doesn't cause seizures' is perfectly structured. Each beat tops the last. Very character-specific.

jokes.text: Pete reports Sebastian the producer 'OD'd last night in Guy Fieri's apartment.' Jenna: 'Oh, my God, that's terrible.' Pete: 'Terrible for me.'
jokes.setup: Pete reports a producer has overdosed
jokes.punchline: Jenna's performative concern ('Oh, my God, that's terrible') immediately echoed by Pete's pivot to pure self-interest ('Terrible for me')
jokes.explanation: The Guy Fieri detail is a perfect absurdist specificity, and the 'terrible for me' pivot is a tight, well-executed selfishness joke. The mirrored 'Oh, my God, that's terrible' structure (Jenna says it sincerely, Pete immediately restates it with his own spin) is economical and effective.

jokes.text: Jenna: 'I'm having Sebastian's lucky earring sent from the morgue. Wear it.'
jokes.setup: Jenna needs Pete to replace the deceased producer
jokes.punchline: She's already arranged to have a dead man's earring retrieved from his corpse as a good luck charm, and orders Pete to wear it
jokes.explanation: Jenna's casual morbidity is perfectly in character. 'Wear it' as a command after explaining where it came from (a morgue) is darkly funny. The efficiency — stating a completely insane thing as though it's routine — is excellent.

jokes.text: Paul is on 'a transvestite cruise for the last month. It's called Caribbean Queens — for emphasis, No More Love on the Run.'
jokes.setup: Someone asks if Jenna is spending Valentine's with Paul
jokes.punchline: Paul is on a transvestite cruise literally named after a Billy Ocean song, and she explains the name is 'for emphasis'
jokes.explanation: Layered joke: the cruise name is a Billy Ocean reference, but explained deadpan as 'for emphasis' suggesting the cruise is deliberately making a point. The Billy Ocean legal subplot is an unexpected world-expanding detail.

jokes.text: 'Billy Ocean is furious, and very litigious. But he's powerless as long as they stay in international waters.'
jokes.setup: Jenna explained the transvestite cruise is named after a Billy Ocean song
jokes.punchline: Billy Ocean has pursued legal action but they've found a maritime law loophole — the absurdity of a transvestite cruise evading Billy Ocean lawsuits via international waters
jokes.explanation: Escalates the previous joke brilliantly. Billy Ocean as 'furious and litigious' is unexpected; 'powerless as long as they stay in international waters' treats a maritime law technicality as the logical solution to a Billy Ocean copyright dispute involving transvestites. Perfect 30 Rock absurdist logic chain.

jokes.text: Frank on picking up women at Ikea: 'I've gotten women there two, three points hotter than me. So, you know...fours.'
jokes.setup: Frank brags about picking up women two or three points hotter than him at Ikea
jokes.punchline: The reveal that Frank rates himself so low that 'two or three points hotter' still only lands him fours
jokes.explanation: Brilliantly constructed self-deprecation. The brag sets up an expectation that the punchline will involve attractive women; instead it reveals Frank's self-image is so low that his 'upgrades' are still fours. The structure is airtight — the pause before 'fours' is doing essential work. Maximum funny per word. Genuinely exceptional joke. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Liz coins 'Saint lame-entine's nay' and immediately says 'Oh, honey, that sucks.'
jokes.setup: Liz tries to make a portmanteau mocking Valentine's Day
jokes.punchline: She attempts the pun, recognizes it's terrible, and immediately sympathizes with herself: 'Oh, honey, that sucks'
jokes.explanation: The joke is the meta-awareness of the bad pun — Liz immediately self-critiques. 'Oh, honey, that sucks' as self-directed sympathy is a deeply character-specific Liz Lemon move. Similar in structure to Jack's 'I've had two coffees' (joke 13) but more self-pitying.

jokes.text: Liz says 'We better be able to survive a simple trip to Ikea.' Jack/colleague: 'No, Liz, don't test it. Especially this early in a relationship. It's like when Mickey Rourke tested his catapult on me.'
jokes.setup: Liz insists they can handle Ikea as a couple
jokes.punchline: The warning is illustrated by an insane non-sequitur: Mickey Rourke testing a catapult on Jack Donaghy
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Mickey Rourke tested his catapult on me' as a cautionary tale about not testing relationships is perfectly absurdist. Jack's implication that he has personal experience being used as a catapult test subject by Mickey Rourke is wonderfully strange. 'Wow, I was almost listening' as Liz's response is a perfect button.

jokes.text: Kenneth gives Jenna a pube count update: 'We'll take a pube count, but it doesn't feel worth it.'
jokes.setup: Jenna had Hazel take an experimental medication that was supposed to remove pubic hair
jokes.punchline: Kenneth dutifully reports on the pube situation as if it's routine page business
jokes.explanation: Functional callback that gets Kenneth's earnest professionalism into the pubic hair territory. 'Doesn't feel worth it' is the right deflating coda. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Jack's golf frustration aside: 'Maybe I'm hitting them too hard. And I should not have walked past that sporting goods store where the mannequins have nipples. And what race were those mannequins, because their skin was gray. They were like faceless sex aliens.'
jokes.setup: Jack is struggling with his pent-up energy (sexual frustration)
jokes.punchline: His stream-of-consciousness spirals from golf to mannequin nipples to a meditation on the race of gray mannequins to 'faceless sex aliens'
jokes.explanation: Escalating absurdist monologue from Jack that reveals the depth of his frustration. 'Faceless sex aliens' is a great image. The structural escalation (too hard → mannequin nipples → race of mannequins → sex aliens) each beat topping the last is classic 30 Rock dense joke stacking.

jokes.text: Diana talks to her dead husband: 'Wonderful news. You know our pacing horse, squanto? She's foaling in the spring.' Jack: 'Your husband has been dead for 15 years.'
jokes.setup: Diana keeps using 'we' to refer to herself and her decisions, Jack corrects her that her husband is dead
jokes.punchline: Diana responds to the news of her husband's death by immediately pivoting to cheerful horse breeding news directed at the dead man
jokes.explanation: Perfect WASP denial comedy. Diana's response to being reminded her husband is dead is to cheerfully update him on the pacing horse as if he might be interested. The name 'Squanto' is an excellent absurdist touch. Establishes Diana's character efficiently.

jokes.text: Diana: 'What about organizing three round-Robin paddle tennis tournaments?' / 'I heard that one of them was a disaster.' / 'Who told you that? Bebe Butler? Oh, she's trying to destroy me.'
jokes.setup: Jack is explaining that extracting someone from North Korea is harder than organizing a paddle tennis tournament
jokes.punchline: Diana is deeply offended by the comparison, then deflects into social warfare with Bebe Butler — treating a WASP social rivalry as equivalent to geopolitical crisis
jokes.explanation: Good character-building joke for Diana — her world of paddle tennis tournaments and social enemies is just as serious to her as international diplomacy. 'Bebe Butler is trying to destroy me' is delivered with the weight of a geopolitical accusation.

jokes.text: Jack's UN speech failures: 'Mein herr, meine frau Avery Jessup... Kim Jong-Il vuvuzela / Charlize Theron... Boomerang my Sheila back to her Joey, mate.'
jokes.setup: Jack claims he's been to the UN repeatedly to advocate for Avery's release
jokes.punchline: His UN speeches are revealed as a series of mangled foreign-language attempts — German, vague Korean/South African, Australian — none of which are coherent
jokes.explanation: 'Boomerang my Sheila back to her Joey, mate' is a fantastic line — Jack's attempt at Australian diplomacy is hilariously mangled slang. The accumulation of three failed linguistic attempts, each from a completely different country (Germany, North Korea/South Africa, Australia) reveals Jack's incompetence in a very funny way. High quotability for the Australian line especially.

jokes.text: Jack: 'The U.N. is a useless organization, with a ridiculous army. Robin's egg blue helmets? Great camouflage, if you're invading an easter egg hunt.'
jokes.setup: Jack dismisses the UN as useless
jokes.punchline: He focuses his critique on UN peacekeeping helmets' color — 'robin's egg blue' — and concludes they're only good for invading an Easter egg hunt
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Great camouflage, if you're invading an Easter egg hunt' is a perfectly structured punchline — the setup (robin's egg blue helmets) pays off with a specific, vivid, instantly quotable image. The structure is textbook: build the premise, subvert with the smallest possible scenario. Highly quotable and very Jack Donaghy. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Diana delivers a perfect Australian insult: 'Strewth, what a bull-dingered Valentine's Day.' Then: 'Oh, and Jack? I speak Australian.'
jokes.setup: Jack has just demonstrated his broken Australian ('Boomerang my Sheila back to her Joey, mate') and Diana has been listening throughout
jokes.punchline: Diana reveals she herself speaks fluent Australian, having used it to insult Jack's Valentine's Day without him knowing, then calmly discloses this as she exits
jokes.explanation: Perfectly timed payoff. Diana deploys Australian slang as a secret weapon, then reveals her fluency as a casual exit line — 'I speak Australian' as if it's perfectly normal. The exit timing is excellent. Establishes Diana as formidable and surprising. The joke is earned because we've seen Jack struggle with Australian moments before.

jokes.text: Liz and Criss pass a fighting couple in Ikea: 'I wish I'd died on Iwo Jima and never met you.' Criss: 'Whoa. What was that?' Liz: 'Not us.'
jokes.setup: Liz and Criss arrive at Ikea trying to stay positive
jokes.punchline: An unseen couple is audibly fighting — 'I wish I'd died on Iwo Jima and never met you' — which Liz immediately distinguishes from their own relationship
jokes.explanation: 'I wish I'd died on Iwo Jima and never met you' is a wonderfully specific, historically-grounded insult that escalates the Ikea couple-fighting trope to maximum. The historical specificity (Iwo Jima rather than just 'died') makes it genuinely funny. 'Not us' as Liz's flat denial is a perfect deadpan button.

jokes.text: Liz says 'I just got my period' mid-conversation as a non-sequitur
jokes.setup: Criss is rallying Liz about their Ikea plan
jokes.punchline: Liz's response to inspirational relationship talk is to announce she just got her period
jokes.explanation: Decent anti-romantic non-sequitur. The comic timing is good but the joke itself is fairly thin — it's mostly funny for the abruptness. Functional but not crafted.

jokes.text: After tension between Liz and Criss in Ikea, a stranger says 'So tense. Just like my mom's back.' Then immediately: 'I'm going back to those cute bowls.' / 'I swear to God, I will stab you!'
jokes.setup: Liz and Criss's first Ikea tension moment
jokes.punchline: A random stranger comments on their tension; Criss's innocent pivot to bowls; Liz threatening to stab him
jokes.explanation: Three-beat joke: stranger's quirky aside ('just like my mom's back'), Criss's oblivious pivot to bowls, and Liz's violent escalation. The escalation to stabbing is the punchline. Good Ikea chaos energy.

jokes.text: Tracy's Valentine's Day pickup philosophy: 'Valentine's Day is the perfect time to meet vulnerable women. It's scumbag Christmas!'
jokes.setup: Tracy shares his predatory Valentine's Day strategy with Lutz
jokes.punchline: 'Scumbag Christmas' as a rebranding of Valentine's Day from the pickup artist's perspective
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best single-line jokes. 'Scumbag Christmas' is an instantly legendary coinage — perfectly economical (two words), highly quotable, and a genuinely original reframe of Valentine's Day. It captures the entire premise of the Tracy/Frank/Lutz subplot in two words. Perfectly character-specific for Tracy Jordan. Justifies the 8+ score.

jokes.text: Tracy lists vulnerable women locations: 'Cat shelters, blood banks, the ice cream stand at a Celtic woman concert... And we strike.'
jokes.setup: Tracy advises Lutz on where to find vulnerable women on Valentine's Day
jokes.punchline: The escalating specificity of locations — from plausible (cat shelters) to oddly specific (ice cream stand at a Celtic Woman concert)
jokes.explanation: The Celtic Woman concert ice cream stand is the punchline — the specificity is perfect. Each location in the list is funnier than the last. 'And we strike' delivered with predatory gravity after such a mundane list is a good tonal joke.

jokes.text: Tracy's beauty salon strategy: 'We go to the beauty salon where white girls try to do black hair. Sisters come out crying, feeling all bad about themselves, and we walk up on them all, Hey, baby, what's wrong?'
jokes.setup: Tracy continues his vulnerable women location guide
jokes.punchline: The specific scenario of white beauty salons botching Black hair, with the predatory 'Hey, baby, what's wrong?' — which also plants the episode's title
jokes.explanation: This joke earns a rewatch bonus because it plants the episode title and the repeated refrain. The racial dynamics add some edge (dark subversive) and it's very Tracy-specific. The episode title plant is a structural bonus.

jokes.text: Tracy on Lutz's romantic prospects: 'After we watch Fievel Goes West, we're gonna get you some action.'
jokes.setup: Tracy promises Lutz 'the adventure of a lifetime'
jokes.punchline: The adventure begins with watching Fievel Goes West — a 1991 children's animated movie — as prep for romantic conquest
jokes.explanation: The absurd specificity of Fievel Goes West as inspirational pre-game viewing is a classic Tracy Jordan non-sequitur. 'Adventure of a lifetime' → Fievel Goes West is a perfect anti-climactic pivot.

jokes.text: Jenna's paranoid rant about America's Kidz Got Singing: 'It's not some rinky-dink late night show that a bald idiot produces.' Then: 'Tomorrow night on America's Kidz Got Singing, the judge becomes the opposite of the judge.'
jokes.setup: Jenna is anxious about her live singing performance
jokes.punchline: She insults TGS (and Pete) via a left-handed compliment, then tries to sound profound with 'the judge becomes the opposite of the judge' — which is empty
jokes.explanation: Jenna's narcissism is well-deployed: she manages to insult TGS (and Pete) while ostensibly talking about herself, and her attempt at a profound tagline is hollow. Character-specific but not especially crafted.

jokes.text: Jenna coins 'jiumph' — 'which is short for Jenna triumph' — as a word that needs to happen tonight.
jokes.setup: Jenna demands the night be a success
jokes.punchline: She's invented a portmanteau of her own name and 'triumph,' treating it as an established word while defining it
jokes.explanation: Classic Jenna narcissism — inserting her name into a word as if it's natural. The fact that she defines it immediately ('which is short for Jenna triumph') reveals the insecurity beneath the confidence. Very character-specific.

jokes.text: Jack and Diana at the UN: The UN bureaucrat says 'Yes, your excellency. And I also wish you, a bear-y happy Valentine's Day.' He holds up a bear.
jokes.setup: Jack is at the UN trying to conduct serious diplomatic business on Valentine's Day
jokes.punchline: The UN bureaucrat presents a bear as a Valentine's Day greeting — 'bear-y' happy — completely undercutting the gravity of the setting
jokes.explanation: Good situational irony — the UN's solemn atmosphere punctured by a literal Valentine's teddy bear and a pun. The visual gag (holding up the bear) is the punchline.

jokes.text: Jack looks at his watch, sees '14' (the date), says 'Do you see a 14 on my watch? / Yes, it's the date. Happy Valentine's Day. That's cute.'
jokes.setup: Jack is dismissing military time (14:30) as un-American
jokes.punchline: The '14' he points to is the date on his watch — and Diana gently points this out while complimenting it as 'cute'
jokes.explanation: Well-structured classic misdirection joke. Jack's confident anti-metric/anti-military-time stance is undercut by the reveal that he confused the date for the hour. Diana's 'That's cute' is a perfect one-note putdown.

jokes.text: Jack: 'I've organized several dog and pony shows, and I'm offended by what you're implying.' Diana takes offense at Jack's metaphor; she literally organizes dog and pony shows.
jokes.setup: Jack uses 'dog and pony show' as a dismissive idiom for UN theater
jokes.punchline: Diana takes it literally — she organizes actual dog and pony shows and is professionally offended
jokes.explanation: Clean misdirection with excellent character work. The idiom/literal inversion is a classic comedy device but executed here with perfect WASP specificity — of course Diana Jessup literally organizes dog and pony shows. This joke also plants a callback used multiple times later in the episode.

jokes.text: Diana: 'We both married much, much older men, which can be hard, or, more often, flaccid.'
jokes.setup: Diana is listing things she and Jack have in common
jokes.punchline: The pivot from 'hard' (meaning difficult) to 'flaccid' (implying their elderly husbands' impotence) is a sudden tonal shift into frank sexual territory
jokes.explanation: Exceptional single-line joke. The structure is perfect: 'which can be hard' sets up a straightforward observation about marrying older men, then 'or, more often, flaccid' pivots the meaning completely. The WASP character who would never normally discuss impotence dropping this with perfect calm is a great character subversion. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: The GPS tracker for Tracy's lizard Jeremy says he's inside the room — and the lizard is attached to Hazel's face, 'mating with my mouth.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth mentions Tracy's GPS-collared lizard Jeremy who keeps escaping and biting people
jokes.punchline: The GPS reveals the lizard is 'right on top of us' — cut to it apparently attempting to mate with Hazel's mouth
jokes.explanation: Well-escalated physical gag. The GPS thriller-style 'three feet, two feet, right on top of us' builds tension that pays off with the absurd lizard-on-face visual. 'He's mating with my mouth' / 'He likes you!' is a funny button with Kenneth's earnestness.

jokes.text: Tracy's Father's Day strip club tip: 'Go to a strip club on Father's Day, and shout things like, I'm proud of you!'
jokes.setup: Tracy is sharing unconventional tips for meeting vulnerable women
jokes.punchline: Targeting strip clubs on Father's Day with paternal affirmations — 'I'm proud of you!' — as an unexpected and darkly sweet manipulation
jokes.explanation: Genuinely brilliant dark comedy. The combination of Father's Day + strip club + 'I'm proud of you!' creates an entire emotional backstory (daddy issues) in a single joke with maximum compression. It's simultaneously dark, funny, and oddly touching. Original concept executed with perfect economy. 'Classic.' as the response is the perfect button. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Tracy's department store swimsuit switcheroo: switching size-6 tags to size-12, then consoling the woman who comes out thinking she's gotten bigger with 'Hey, baby, what's wrong?'
jokes.setup: Tracy lists another method for creating vulnerable women to approach
jokes.punchline: Deliberately sabotaging swimsuit sizing to manufacture emotional vulnerability, then exploiting it
jokes.explanation: Disturbing and funny in equal measure. The meticulous planning behind the strategy (a fully narrated con) and the deadpan execution make this work as dark comedy. The 'Hey, baby, what's wrong?' callback gives it structural purpose.

jokes.text: Jenna on Weight Watchers: 'I did Watchers to stay pageant-fit, but it was too much math for a six-year-old. Thank God I found cigarettes.'
jokes.setup: Tracy mentions Weight Watchers as a good place to meet vulnerable women
jokes.punchline: Jenna's Weight Watchers experience: she was six years old, doing it for pageants, and found cigarettes as the preferable alternative diet method
jokes.explanation: Excellent character joke. Every element lands: the child pageant world, Weight Watchers being 'too much math for a six-year-old,' and cigarettes as the rational alternative. It builds Jenna's disturbing backstory in two sentences with perfect economy. 'Thank God I found cigarettes' is a beautifully dark button. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Tracy demonstrates making a woman feel vulnerable by throwing a bowl of cereal on a woman and asking 'Oh, baby, did someone throw cereal on you? Let's get you out of these wet clothes.'
jokes.setup: Tracy says 'if worse comes to worse, make the lady feel vulnerable. Check this out.'
jokes.punchline: He throws cereal on a woman and immediately pivots to a seduction line — making the vulnerability himself, then immediately exploiting it
jokes.explanation: Physical gag with a dark comic twist — the 'vulnerability creation' system has a direct-action shortcut. The woman's angry reaction ('What is wrong with you people?') followed by 'Whatever. Jeremy says she's a tease anyway' is a great unexpected button (blaming the lizard).

jokes.text: The woman rejects Tracy's cereal pickup: 'What is wrong with you people?' Tracy: 'Whatever. Jeremy says she's a tease anyway.'
jokes.setup: Tracy's cereal gambit has failed spectacularly
jokes.punchline: He deflects rejection by citing the opinion of his pet lizard as social authority
jokes.explanation: Tracy attributing judgmental opinions to his lizard Jeremy is a perfect absurdist character button. 'Jeremy says she's a tease anyway' treats the lizard as a social arbiter and deflects responsibility brilliantly. Extremely economical.

jokes.text: Liz finds salt-and-pepper shakers: 'You put them together, it makes a heart. Take them apart, two red sperms.'
jokes.setup: Criss is trying to find romantic items at Ikea
jokes.punchline: The salt and pepper shakers are both a romantic heart AND two sperms depending on configuration — noted with equal enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: Good visual observation joke. The dual-nature of the shakers (romantic heart vs. two sperms) delivered with the same enthusiastic energy is funny. Criss's delight at 'two red sperms' as a bonus feature is character-specific.

jokes.text: The Ikea section title card appears: 'Ikea.' [28 seconds of scene establishment]
jokes.setup: The show is going to an Ikea sequence
jokes.punchline: 30 Rock uses a title card that simply says 'Ikea.' — acknowledging the setting with self-aware gravity, as if Ikea itself is a character
jokes.explanation: 30 Rock's use of the single-word title card for comedic effect — treating Ikea as a mythic destination. Mostly structural/visual and lands as a setup for the whole subplot rather than a standalone joke.

jokes.text: Transylvanian consul: 'I am from Transylvania, but I am not a vampire. I'm just a night owl with a terrible garlic allergy. So, this is regarding that boy who went missing in my castle?'
jokes.setup: Jack and Diana are at the Transylvanian consulate at the UN
jokes.punchline: The consul denies being a vampire but then (a) admits to a garlic allergy, (b) refers to a missing boy in his castle — both of which suggest he is, in fact, a vampire
jokes.explanation: Beautifully constructed joke. The structure is: denial → immediate evidence of the thing denied → second, more damning evidence. The garlic allergy is funny; 'that boy who went missing in my castle' is the escalated punchline that fully commits to the vampire bit. High quotability, excellent structure. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Diana: 'So why the fudge isn't everyone fudging freaking the fudge out!'
jokes.setup: Diana is passionately arguing that Avery deserves more attention because she's 'a beautiful white American'
jokes.punchline: Her passionate speech is almost all censored by her own inability to swear — she uses 'fudge' three times as a replacement, maintaining her WASP propriety while raging
jokes.explanation: Callback and escalation of Diana's inability to swear. The triple 'fudge' is a running joke structure within a single sentence — she keeps trying to be profane and keeps substituting 'fudge.' The comedic density of three instances in one outburst is strong structural work. Deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: Jack threatens the consul: 'I am a very powerful man. I can see to it that Transylvania never sees another episode of Friends. / No! Monica and Chandler just slept together in London.'
jokes.setup: Jack is trying to intimidate the Transylvanian consul into apologizing
jokes.punchline: His ultimate diplomatic leverage is threatening to cut off Friends — which works instantly, because the consul is horrified he'd miss the Chandler/Monica London hook-up
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The concept of using Friends as geopolitical leverage is wonderfully absurd; the consul's panicked response ('No! Monica and Chandler just slept together in London!') makes it perfect. The Friends reference is specific enough (the London episode is a real, beloved episode) to land with knowing audiences. Beautifully structured: outrageous threat → instant, specific, panicked capitulation. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Jack's Friends spoiler as negotiating weapon: 'Oh, and Cjokula — at Monica and Chandler's wedding, Rachel's the one who is pregnant.'
jokes.setup: Jack has successfully coerced the consul and is leaving with Diana
jokes.punchline: As a parting shot, Jack spoils the Friends wedding episode — weaponizing a TV spoiler as a final power move
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best joke. Building on the Friends leverage joke, Jack escalates to a spoiler as a parting punishment — using his superior knowledge of Friends to hurt the consul one final time. 'Cjokula' (Count Dracula + joke name) is a great throwaway. The spoiler itself ('Rachel's the one who is pregnant') is a real Friends moment delivered with perfect vindictive calm. The structure of saving this for the exit is theatrically perfect. This is a genuinely exceptional piece of comedy writing.

jokes.text: Ikea table fight becomes a relationship metaphor: 'Maybe a more fun table would be a better table for me.' 'Well, maybe a more fun table wouldn't be as supportive.' 'No no no, we are not letting this table be a metaphor for our relationship. That's what Ikea WANTS us to do.'
jokes.setup: They've found the table they planned to get, but Criss isn't sure about it
jokes.punchline: They slip into using the table as a relationship metaphor ('supportive'); Liz catches it and blames Ikea for the manipulation
jokes.explanation: Sharp observational comedy about how Ikea trips reveal relationship dynamics. Liz's 'That's what Ikea wants us to do' transforms a cliché into a conspiracy theory, which is very Liz. The joke works on the meta-level too — the show IS using the table as a metaphor, and Liz's awareness of it doesn't stop it from working.

jokes.text: The table metaphor fight: Liz and Criss argue about the table being 'uptight' vs. 'fun', then: 'I'm just not sure my chair wants to be with this table.' / 'Why, because deep down your chair would rather be with other chairs?'
jokes.setup: Liz is committed to the Kurtz table; Criss thinks it's too uptight
jokes.punchline: Both characters commit to the table-as-relationship metaphor despite explicitly calling it out
jokes.explanation: The Ikea table-as-relationship metaphor is well-executed extended cringe comedy. The joke is that both acknowledge 'we are not doing this' (Liz: 'We are not letting this table be a metaphor for our relationship. That's what Ikea wants us to do') and then immediately continue the metaphor. 'Deep down your chair would rather be with other chairs' is a good escalation.

jokes.text: Liz: 'Well, it's just the table thinks the chair takes too many camping trips with Richard.'
jokes.setup: Liz and Criss are using furniture as proxies for their relationship anxieties
jokes.punchline: Liz introduces 'Richard' — an apparently real person the chair/Criss goes camping with — revealing a real relationship insecurity through the metaphor
jokes.explanation: Good escalation within the extended metaphor. The introduction of 'Richard' as a third party through the furniture metaphor — implying real jealousy disguised as furniture talk — is character-true and escalates the emotional stakes. The specificity of 'camping trips' is nicely absurd.

jokes.text: Liz and Criss walk through the Ikea warehouse and Criss sees a T-shirt: 'Seriously? Zoo York.'
jokes.setup: Liz calls them a team and cheers 'To the warehouse!'
jokes.punchline: Criss's immediate flat reaction to a Zoo York branded item in Ikea — 'Seriously? Zoo York.' — deflates the momentary camaraderie
jokes.explanation: Quick throwaway visual gag — functional but thin. The absurdity of finding Zoo York merchandise in Ikea is mildly funny, and the flat delivery works. But it's a minor beat.

jokes.text: Criss: 'Seriously? Zoo York.' — reacting to something Liz is wearing in Ikea
jokes.setup: They're making their way to the warehouse section
jokes.punchline: Criss is judgmentally reacting to Liz wearing a 'Zoo York' branded item (a knockoff streetwear brand)
jokes.explanation: Quick Liz fashion joke. 'Zoo York' as a specific brand choice for Liz Lemon is accurate character comedy, but the joke is more of an aside than a fully realized bit.

jokes.text: Jenna refuses a live band: 'I have made love to Alfonso, he can't keep rhythm, get him out of here.' / 'That's a wrap on Alfonso. Alfonso Disparioso, everybody.'
jokes.setup: Jenna demands no live band for her performance
jokes.punchline: She justifies this by revealing she's slept with Alfonso and he's bad at rhythm — Pete dismisses the band member with a showbiz send-off ('Alfonso Disparioso, everybody')
jokes.explanation: Jenna using her sexual history as professional criteria is perfect character comedy. Pete's 'Alfonso Disparioso, everybody' as a dignified send-off for the casually dismissed musician is a great deadpan button — giving the bit a showbiz formality it doesn't deserve.

jokes.text: Jenna to herself in the mirror: 'This is your moment. The world breathes for you. I love you, myself.'
jokes.setup: Jenna is psyching herself up before her performance
jokes.punchline: 'I love you, myself' — she refers to herself in the third person as if herself is a separate beloved entity
jokes.explanation: 'I love you, myself' is an excellent character line — the grammar is both correct (addressing herself) and narcissistically weird. The sequence ('the world breathes for you') builds Jenna's delusional self-regard to a perfect peak.

jokes.text: Jenna mouths along to her own playback but isn't singing — her mouth moves but no sound. Pete: 'Jenna, you're not singing.' Jenna: 'Yes, I am.'
jokes.setup: Jenna has her playback going and is 'performing'
jokes.punchline: She isn't singing — her mouth moves silently — but she insists she is, either in denial or genuinely confused
jokes.explanation: Good visual/character comedy — Jenna's complete denial of objective reality ('Yes, I am' when clearly not singing) is perfectly character-specific. It establishes the 'yips' problem while generating a laugh from her obliviousness.

jokes.text: Jack: 'I didn't know you had that in you. Yosemite Sam was based on my grandfather, so yes, I do have a temper.'
jokes.setup: Jack compliments Diana on her fierceness at the UN
jokes.punchline: Diana casually drops that Yosemite Sam — the cartoon character — was based on her grandfather, explaining her temper
jokes.explanation: Excellent throwaway. The idea that Yosemite Sam (a cartoon character known for explosive anger) is based on Diana's grandfather is wonderfully absurd — and it makes perfect visual sense given Diana's outburst. Delivered as a casual family fact. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Diana: 'In 1978, I was in Playboy, just wearing a necktie and holding hands with a black girl.'
jokes.setup: Jack says there are many things he doesn't know about Diana
jokes.punchline: Diana's unexpected 1978 Playboy appearance — the specific details ('wearing a necktie,' 'holding hands with a black girl') make this a perfect period-piece character revelation
jokes.explanation: Perfectly delivered unexpected revelation. The combination of WASP Diana, 1978 Playboy, a necktie, and 'holding hands with a black girl' (capturing a very specific late-70s progressive-but-still-objectifying aesthetic) is wonderfully specific. This is a great character subversion joke. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Jack apologizes for comparing Diana to her late husband — 'You are not some liver-spotted old man constantly spilling hot tea in his lap until his whole crotch was useless. Useless!'
jokes.setup: Jack is making a romantic speech to Diana, apologizing for earlier comparisons
jokes.punchline: His apology describes her dead husband in graphic, humiliating detail — 'liver-spotted,' 'spilling hot tea in his lap,' 'whole crotch was useless'
jokes.explanation: Wonderful subversion of the romantic speech genre. Jack's 'compliment' to Diana is actually an extended, specific, gleefully cruel portrait of her dead husband's physical deterioration. 'Useless! Useless!' repeated as a button on 'crotch' is a perfect comedic rhythm. Deeply character-specific for Jack's particular brand of backhanded gallantry. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Jack and Diana try to talk about baseball to defuse sexual tension: '- The bats are long and hard. - The gloves are girls. - Balls! - Jeter's thighs in those pants. New topic.'
jokes.setup: Jack and Diana realize they're attracted to each other and try to talk about baseball instead
jokes.punchline: Every baseball term they choose is either sexual ('bats are long and hard') or romantic ('gloves are girls') until 'Jeter's thighs in those pants' makes it worse
jokes.explanation: Brilliantly structured escalation. The rapid-fire exchange — each baseball term immediately sexualized, each attempt to neutralize the conversation making it worse — is textbook 30 Rock joke density. 'Jeter's thighs in those pants' as the climactic failure is perfect. 'New topic' as the shared capitulation is a great button. The structure of this exchange justifies the high score.

jokes.text: Dentist examines Jenna: 'If those teeth were in your vagina, you'd be considered a monster.'
jokes.setup: Jenna is at the dentist; the dentist is examining her mouth
jokes.punchline: The dentist's assessment pivots to an assessment of how the same teeth would be received in a different anatomical location — the 'vagina dentata' reference delivered with clinical calm
jokes.explanation: Unexpected and dark. The 'vagina dentata' concept delivered as a medical observation is a genuinely original comedic frame. The clinical tone makes it funnier than it would be if played edgier. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Doctor to Jenna: 'Unfortunately, there's no field of medicine that deals with the brain. But I can give you a pamphlet for a cult.'
jokes.setup: The doctor tells Jenna her problem is psychosomatic
jokes.punchline: He offers a cult pamphlet as medical advice, because there's 'no field of medicine that deals with the brain' — denying the existence of psychiatry/neurology
jokes.explanation: Excellent absurdist premise. 'No field of medicine that deals with the brain' is a perfect piece of logical inversion — denying the existence of psychiatry/neurology — with the cult pamphlet as the only alternative. Highly quotable and well-structured.

jokes.text: Jenna's 'pressure' speech: 'Pressure is trying to pass for four when you just turned seven, at the Miss Toddler Panama City pageant... crammed into the same five-inch heels you wore the year before, blood pooling in your toes. But you know if you don't win, mom can't fix the hole in the gator fence, so you'll be up all night, stabbing gators.'
jokes.setup: Pete suggests Jenna is under too much pressure; Jenna dismisses this
jokes.punchline: Jenna's competing definition of pressure is an increasingly insane escalation of child-pageant horror — gator fences, blood in toes, stabbing gators
jokes.explanation: One of the best extended joke sequences in the episode. Each element of Jenna's 'pressure' speech tops the last: passing as younger at a child pageant → five-inch heels on a seven-year-old → blood pooling in toes → the gator fence → stabbing gators all night. The logic is internally consistent and perfectly dark. 'Stabbing gators' as the climax of a story about child beauty pageants is genuinely brilliant. Deeply character-specific — only Jenna Maroney has this backstory. Approaches the calibration anchor's level of excellence.

jokes.text: Jenna continues the pressure speech: '...your throat burning from the smoke. You still sing so beautifully that it calms the passengers, so that you and the crew can escape.'
jokes.setup: Jenna's pressure speech continues — performing on a party boat that catches fire
jokes.punchline: She sings to calm passengers specifically so she and the crew can escape — abandoning the passengers mid-performance to escape the fire
jokes.explanation: The second installment of the pressure speech is even more character-specific: Jenna's singing is beautiful enough to save lives, but she uses this power selfishly to enable her own escape while leaving passengers behind. The dark twist ('so that you and the crew can escape') is perfectly placed and character-true. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Jenna's final pressure definition: 'Singing the Yemeni national anthem while a handsome but ruthless general pushes a scimitar into your neck, Kristin Chenoweth's corpse at your feet.'
jokes.setup: The pressure speech continues building
jokes.punchline: The final pressure scenario involves a scimitar-wielding Yemeni general and Kristin Chenoweth's corpse — escalating to maximum international absurdity
jokes.explanation: The climax of the pressure speech. 'Kristin Chenoweth's corpse at your feet' is the standout line — the specific detail of her show-business rival being dead at her feet is wonderfully specific, dark, and character-true (Jenna would know exactly which musical theater star she outlasted). 'Handsome but ruthless general' is doing nice work too. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Pete and Jenna staring at each other: 'Well, there's something weird going on here. You feel that sexual energy too?' / 'I mean, but... it would be wrong to act on it.' / 'Well, it's 5:00 somewhere.'
jokes.setup: After Jenna's pressure speech, Pete and Jenna are in a charged moment
jokes.punchline: Pete's 'it's 5:00 somewhere' as justification for acting on wrong sexual impulses — a non sequitur application of a drinking excuse to adultery
jokes.explanation: Decent cringe comedy setup for the Pete/Jenna tension. 'It's 5:00 somewhere' applied to infidelity rather than drinking is a good inversion of the cliché. Functional but not exceptional — the original joke is slightly worn.

jokes.text: The Kurtz table is sold out. Criss: 'This is why you don't just choose one option.' Liz: 'No, this is why you don't waste 45 minutes wandering around the Valentine's marketplace.'
jokes.setup: Liz and Criss had a plan to get one specific table; they discover it's sold out
jokes.punchline: Each immediately blames the other using their pre-existing relationship conflict styles — Criss for lack of options, Liz for lack of discipline
jokes.explanation: Competent cringe/relationship comedy. The sold-out table as the breaking point is earned dramatically. The mutual blame lands but isn't particularly quotable.

jokes.text: Liz: 'Valentine's is the worst! It's even worse than Earth Day. You just see so many dirty feet in sandals.'
jokes.setup: Liz is venting about Valentine's Day after the table debacle
jokes.punchline: She ranks Earth Day as worse than Valentine's specifically for the 'dirty feet in sandals' visual
jokes.explanation: Classic Liz Lemon specificity. The comparison of Valentine's to Earth Day — and the very specific, very Liz reason for disliking Earth Day (dirty feet in sandals) — is sharp character comedy. The non sequitur escalation is perfectly timed.

jokes.text: Liz: 'You didn't finish law school, it's why you still aren't done filling out your 2010 census.' Criss: 'Well what race am I supposed to check? We all come from Africa.'
jokes.setup: Liz is listing Criss's failures to follow through on things
jokes.punchline: Criss's unfinished 2010 census (years later) is because he's had a sincere philosophical debate with himself about race — 'we all come from Africa'
jokes.explanation: Excellent character joke. 'We all come from Africa' as justification for an incomplete census form is a perfect blend of sincere progressive idealism and comic impracticality. It's instantly quotable and deeply Criss-specific. The detail that he still hasn't filed a 2010 census form (years late) is the setup that makes the punchline land perfectly. Justifies 8.

jokes.text: Criss (to Liz, in the fight): 'You have no kids. The only thing you like about your job is taking home free sodas.'
jokes.setup: Criss is hitting back at Liz for attacking him
jokes.punchline: The specific indictment of Liz's life: no kids, and the best perk of her high-status job is free soda
jokes.explanation: The 'free sodas' detail is perfect — it's the most specific and deflating possible indictment of Liz's career satisfaction. A head writer at a successful TV show, and what she values most is the free Snapple. Excellent Liz Lemon character comedy embedded in a fight scene.

jokes.text: Criss: 'That's why I get out of the nidurgangur in the morning.' Ikea employee: 'It's one of our cheaper beds.'
jokes.setup: Criss makes what sounds like a profundity about why he gets up every day
jokes.punchline: An Ikea employee helpfully clarifies that 'nidurgangur' is just one of their cheaper beds — Criss has been using an Ikea bed name as if it's a profound philosophical concept
jokes.explanation: Brilliant Ikea-specific joke. Criss's broken speech — 'that's why I get out of the nidurgangur in the morning' — sounds like a meaningful metaphor until the Ikea employee's factual correction reveals he's using a bed name as a life philosophy. The deadpan Ikea employee clarification is the perfect delivery vehicle. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Kenneth tells Hazel she made a big mistake by not thanking Tracy for throwing milk at her: 'Tracy Jordan threw milk at you, and you didn't even thank him?'
jokes.setup: Kenneth criticizes Hazel for not appreciating TGS enough
jokes.punchline: His example of her ingratitude is that she failed to thank a celebrity for assaulting her with dairy
jokes.explanation: Kenneth's unwavering celebrity deference reaches absurdist heights — she should be grateful that Tracy Jordan threw milk at her. The inverted logic (assault = honor) is perfectly Kenneth. Callback to the Tracy cereal-throwing sequence.

jokes.text: Kenneth explains the page program mascot: 'Pagey, a piece of paper.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth is lecturing Hazel about the honor and tradition of being a page
jokes.punchline: The mascot of the storied page program is literally a piece of paper named 'Pagey'
jokes.explanation: Quick joke on the grandiosity vs. reality of the page program. 'Pagey, a piece of paper' is delivered with great economy — the anti-climactic simplicity of the mascot is the joke. Kenneth's complete sincerity amplifies it.

jokes.text: Hazel on fame: 'Look at Foxy Knoxy. What did she ever do besides not kill anybody?'
jokes.setup: Hazel is explaining that anyone can be famous today
jokes.punchline: Her example of undeserved fame is Amanda Knox (Foxy Knoxy), framed as 'not killing anybody' — treating an acquittal as an accomplishment worthy of celebrity
jokes.explanation: Sharp cultural commentary. 'What did she ever do besides not kill anybody?' is a wonderfully compressed, darkly funny reframe of Amanda Knox's fame. The logic is perverse but coherent from Hazel's ambition-forward perspective. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Hazel: 'I could have a fragrance, or a line of children's handbags, or be in a reality show with other kooky dumb sluts.'
jokes.setup: Hazel is listing her celebrity ambitions
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from genuine ambitions (fragrance) to an increasingly specific and self-aware description of reality TV — 'kooky dumb sluts' as a category she'd happily join
jokes.explanation: Decent character joke. The escalation to 'kooky dumb sluts' as a coveted demographic is the punchline, delivered without irony. Good character establishment for Hazel's self-awareness/ambition combination.

jokes.text: Hazel: 'Last night, I dreamed a baby ate my hair.'
jokes.setup: Hazel is making an argument for her ambitions
jokes.punchline: Her 'dream' pivot is literal — she had a dream that a baby ate her hair, offered as evidence of... something
jokes.explanation: Good non-sequitur button. 'Last night, I dreamed a baby ate my hair' is irrelevant to everything but delivered as if it's relevant. Economy is its strength.

jokes.text: Kenneth hands Hazel 'page underwear that has been handed down, page to page, for over 70 years.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth tells Hazel she needs to start at the bottom
jokes.punchline: The 'starting at the bottom' is literal — she's given 70-year-old shared underwear as part of the page initiation
jokes.explanation: Kenneth's sincerity about disgusting institutional traditions is perfectly character-specific. 'Handed down, page to page, for over 70 years' for underwear is a beautifully gross escalation of the page-program mythology. The visual implication of ancient shared underwear lands well.

jokes.text: Diana and Jack bond over the Baltimore Philharmonic's decline: 'These days, it's just a boom box and a guy in a crab costume. He gets shot out of a cannon at Ravens games.'
jokes.setup: Jack and Diana are discussing their shared love of classical music
jokes.punchline: The Baltimore Philharmonic has declined to a single boom box and a man in a crab costume who performs as a human cannonball at football games
jokes.explanation: Excellent cultural decline joke. The arc from 'Baltimore Philharmonic' to 'boom box and a guy in a crab costume shot from a cannon at Ravens games' is a perfectly specific arc of institutional deterioration. The crab detail is very Baltimore-specific and funny. High quotability.

jokes.text: 'Now why would anyone use music written by a man dying of syphilis to sell douches.' / 'Because people are getting stupider.'
jokes.setup: Jack and Diana are lamenting the commercialization of classical music
jokes.punchline: Schubert's music being used for douche commercials — the specific pairing of 'dying of syphilis' with 'douches' as a company decision, explained by cultural decline
jokes.explanation: Sharp cultural joke. The syphilis/douche connection is a deliberately gross juxtaposition that's funnier for its specificity (Schubert's final sonata) and Diana's 'because people are getting stupider' is the perfect deadpan button.

jokes.text: Jack/Diana contrast Schubert's accomplishments at 31 with a passing obese man: 'Think how much Schubert accomplished in the 31 years he was alive. Coming through. And then there's, uh, this guy. My taxes are paying for your healthcare! Do a sit-up!'
jokes.setup: Jack and Diana are discussing Schubert's productivity
jokes.punchline: They pivot from praising Schubert's legacy to immediately shaming a random passerby for his weight and presumed healthcare costs
jokes.explanation: Good satirical joke about elite classism. The sudden pivot from high culture (Schubert) to screaming 'Do a sit-up!' at a stranger is a perfect tonal whiplash that reveals Jack and Diana's shared snobbery. The bonding-through-classism angle makes it character-specific.

jokes.text: Lutz: 'Yesterday, I ate all the cheese out of the mouse traps.'
jokes.setup: Frank asks how their boys are doing in the Weight Watchers meeting
jokes.punchline: Lutz's assessment of his 'rough week' is eating bait cheese from mouse traps
jokes.explanation: One of Lutz's best character moments. 'I ate all the cheese out of the mouse traps' as a casual explanation of his week is absurd, specific, and deeply pathetic in a way that's purely Lutz. It's the shortest possible joke that communicates maximum desperation. Perfect economy. High quotability — this is the kind of line people repeat.

jokes.text: 'Hey, baby, what's wrong?' — Lutz tries the line; the woman he approaches is actually a postal worker who just made a delivery and destroys him: 'You're gonna tell me about black lady hair, you Louie Anderson little bitch? Run!'
jokes.setup: Lutz tries the vulnerable-woman pickup line — she came out of a beauty salon looking distressed
jokes.punchline: She's not a customer, she's a postal worker who was just making a delivery; she turns on Lutz ferociously, calling him a 'Louie Anderson little bitch'
jokes.explanation: Perfect payoff to the beauty salon strategy joke. The misdirection (Lutz assumes she's a distressed customer, she's a postal worker) is well-set-up. 'Louie Anderson little bitch' as the specific insult she chooses is inspired — Louie Anderson being an unexpected but perfect comparison for Lutz. The aggressive reversal (Tracy's strategy completely backfires for Lutz) is structurally satisfying. The punchline comparison is genuinely original. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Criss in a lingerie store: 'Are you shopping for someone? Do you know what size she is? / No. I don't know. Maybe. No.' / 'I see. It's okay. I have an Uncle who uses my discount here all the time.'
jokes.setup: Criss is trying to find a romantic Valentine's gift for Liz
jokes.punchline: The store employee's matter-of-fact disclosure that her uncle also buys women's lingerie using her employee discount — normalizing his discomfort without judgment
jokes.explanation: Good cringe comedy with an unexpected darkly comic button. The employee's casual disclosure about her uncle normalizes men buying women's lingerie in a way that's oddly more disturbing. Functional and warm without being exceptional.

jokes.text: Pete's 1982 archery flashback: '...so put down your Rubik's cube, turn off that Yakov Smirnoff standup tape, and set all your swatches to right now. [Pete shoots] I've been shot! Someone run into town and find a payphone!'
jokes.setup: Pete reveals he once had the 'yips' as an Olympic archer
jokes.punchline: His archery 'yips' resulted in him shooting himself; the 1982 period details (Rubik's cube, Yakov Smirnoff, Swatches, payphone) pile up as the punchline arrives
jokes.explanation: Excellent cutaway/flashback gag. The 1982 period details are precisely chosen: Rubik's cube, Yakov Smirnoff standup, Swatches — each one a perfect 1982 artifact. Pete shooting himself and then needing a payphone is a great slapstick payoff. 'Set all your swatches to right now' is an excellent period-appropriate hype phrase. High quotability. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Pete and Jenna's yips 'cure': 'Okay, we don't have a lot of time. So, maybe just by acknowledging the problem, we fixed it? I think we did. I'm cured!'
jokes.setup: Pete explains Jenna needs to address her yips
jokes.punchline: They decide that merely acknowledging the problem has fixed it; Jenna immediately declares herself cured after five seconds of 'treatment'
jokes.explanation: Good structural joke — the 'maybe we fixed it?' is a hopeful non-solution that sets up the immediate failure. Jenna's instant overconfidence ('I'm cured!') before the reveal that it's worse is well-timed.

jokes.text: Jenna's cure fails: '#Just you and I / It's worse. I can't open my mouth.'
jokes.setup: Jenna declared herself cured moments ago
jokes.punchline: She literally cannot open her mouth to sing — the yips have physically manifested
jokes.explanation: Clean payoff on the 'cure' joke. 'It's worse. I can't open my mouth.' is perfectly economical. The physical manifestation (jaw locked shut) tops the previous symptom (silent mouthing). Good escalation.

jokes.text: Italian restaurant owner: 'You are like pasta, and a mouth.' / 'The only but we speak of tonight, is the butt of the human ass.'
jokes.setup: A restaurant owner tries to bring Liz and Jack inside by complimenting them as a couple
jokes.punchline: His romantic comparisons are bizarrely specific ('pasta and a mouth') and his pivot from 'but...' to 'butt of the human ass' is a gleefully crude misdirection
jokes.explanation: 'Pasta and a mouth' as a romantic comparison is wonderfully absurd. 'The only but we speak of tonight is the butt of the human ass' is a good wordplay pivot that transforms 'but' into 'butt' — crude but executed with committed absurdism.

jokes.text: The restaurant has 'a unisex bathroom, with, come si dice, no lock, and extra mirrors.'
jokes.setup: The owner is listing the restaurant's romantic amenities
jokes.punchline: The Valentine's perk is an unlocked bathroom with extra mirrors — implying specific sexual activities without stating them
jokes.explanation: Good dark suggestive joke. 'Come si dice' (how do you say) before 'no lock, and extra mirrors' implies the owner can't find words for what the bathroom is for. The pause and the specific details (no lock + extra mirrors) make the implication funny without explicit statement.

jokes.text: Lutz in Ikea parking lot, Frank's backstory: 'Back in the day, you know how many women me and Lamar Odom's dad picked up here? And keep in mind, back then this was a marsh, where people came to shoot at fish.'
jokes.setup: Frank is giving Lutz a final pep talk in the Ikea parking lot
jokes.punchline: His nostalgic pickup story involves Lamar Odom's father and takes place in what was then a fish-shooting marsh
jokes.explanation: 'Lamar Odom's dad' as Frank's pickup partner is a wonderfully specific, unexpected celebrity connection. The historical detail that the Ikea was once 'a marsh where people came to shoot at fish' is a perfect absurdist local history footnote. Good dense joke.

jokes.text: Lutz hits on Liz with 'Hey, baby, what's wrong?' Liz's reaction; Frank: 'About time. The last six years has been like watching Moonlighting.'
jokes.setup: Lutz approaches the distressed woman in the Ikea parking lot with the practiced line
jokes.punchline: The woman is Liz Lemon, his boss; Frank's comment that the last six years has been 'like watching Moonlighting' implies everyone saw Lutz's unrequited feelings before now
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural payoff. The episode-title refrain is used for its climactic misdirection: Lutz uses the line on his own boss. Frank's 'like watching Moonlighting' (the show famous for unresolved sexual tension) is a great pop-culture button. The entire subplot resolves in a satisfying comedic twist.

jokes.text: Liz's realization: 'I'm female Lutz.' Lutz: 'I love you too.' Liz: 'No, I mean... I'm my own worst enemy.' / 'Also I menstruate a lot.'
jokes.setup: Liz realizes she and Lutz have the same self-sabotaging pattern
jokes.punchline: Lutz misinterprets 'female Lutz' as a love confession; then Liz adds 'Also I menstruate a lot' as a further self-description, undercutting her insight
jokes.explanation: Excellent character beat. 'I'm female Lutz' is a cutting self-assessment; Lutz's 'I love you too' misinterpretation is a great beat; and 'Also I menstruate a lot' as a Liz addition to her own character description is wonderfully specific self-deprecation. The menstruation callback (she mentioned it earlier in the episode) adds structural cohesion. Justifies 8.

jokes.text: Liz: 'You want to know the reason why Lutz is alone? Lutz! And Dollhouse penis syndrome.' Lutz's horrified reaction.
jokes.setup: The group is discussing why Lutz is alone
jokes.punchline: Frank announces 'Dollhouse penis syndrome' as one of the reasons — with zero explanation — to Lutz's apparent horror
jokes.explanation: The unexplained 'Dollhouse penis syndrome' as a medical condition is original and funny — it works precisely because it's never explained. The reaction from Lutz suggests it's real and mortifying. Maximum comedy per word.

jokes.text: Liz's realization complaints: 'Oh, realizations are the worst.'
jokes.setup: Liz has had an uncomfortable moment of self-awareness
jokes.punchline: Her complaint isn't that the realization is wrong, but that realizations themselves are inconvenient
jokes.explanation: Perfect Liz Lemon four-word joke. 'Realizations are the worst' treats self-awareness as an inconvenience comparable to bad weather. Maximum character specificity in minimum words.

jokes.text: Frank's Valentine's payoff: 'Worse than me trying to send a fax.' / 'I spent Valentine's with friends. / We are work acquaintances at best. At worst, we are rivals who inspire and try to make each other better.'
jokes.setup: The three men assess their Valentine's Day
jokes.punchline: Tracy's emotional redefinition of friendship: 'rivals who inspire and try to make each other better' — framing male friendship in the most competitive possible terms
jokes.explanation: Strong character button for the Tracy/Frank/Lutz subplot. Tracy's insistence on the most arms-length possible description of friendship ('at worst, rivals who inspire') while clearly caring about Lutz is character-true and emotionally resonant in a funny way.

jokes.text: Tracy's Valentine's obligation reveal: 'Right now, Angie's in a hotel room dressed as a clown. And I'm supposed to get into an elephant costume and interview her for a job at the circus.'
jokes.setup: Tracy reveals he abandoned his Valentine's plans to help Lutz
jokes.punchline: The Valentine's activity he skipped: a clown/elephant roleplay scenario involving a fake job interview at a circus
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Tracy abandoned his Valentine's plans — which were extraordinary — to help Lutz. The specificity of 'Angie in a clown costume, Tracy interviewing her for a circus job in an elephant costume' is the most Tracy Jordan Valentine's Day conceivable. The detail that it's a 'job interview at the circus' within the roleplay adds a layer of bureaucratic absurdism. Highly quotable. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: 'Now let's go get some tiny meatballs.' / 'Meatballs, here we come!' / 'Meatballs!'
jokes.setup: Tracy gives a rallying speech about friendship
jokes.punchline: The emotional climax of the friendship subplot is immediately followed by enthusiastic agreement to eat tiny Ikea meatballs — deflating the sentiment
jokes.explanation: Good anti-climactic button. The pivot from 'rivals who inspire each other' to immediate enthusiasm for Ikea meatballs deflates the sentiment in a classically 30 Rock way. 'Meatballs, here we come!' as a rallying cry is funny in its smallness.

jokes.text: Jack's confession to Liz: 'I want to have sex with Avery's mother.' / 'No! You can't do that.' / 'And come on, didn't our friends the ancient Olmecs bed both mother and daughter to satisfy their Jaguar gods? And everybody loves them.'
jokes.setup: Jack reveals his attraction to Diana to Liz for moral guidance
jokes.punchline: Jack attempts to justify mother/daughter attraction by citing Olmec mythology — 'and everybody loves them' as the logical conclusion
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character comedy. Jack using ancient Olmec mythology to justify inappropriate attraction — presented with complete logical confidence — is brilliantly absurd. 'And everybody loves them' as the closing argument is perfectly illogical. Only Jack Donaghy would pivot to Mesoamerican anthropology to rationalize wanting to sleep with his missing wife's mother. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Liz walking up stairs while on phone with Jack: 'Just hearing your labored breathing while you walk up stairs has purged me of all sexual desire.'
jokes.setup: Jack has been moved by Liz's moral guidance
jokes.punchline: It's not Liz's wisdom but her huffing and puffing on the stairs that has de-aroused Jack
jokes.explanation: Perfect character beat. Liz's stair-huffing as an anti-aphrodisiac — better than any moral argument — is perfectly character-specific for both: Jack's fastidious disgust for physical weakness and Liz's hapless embodiment. 'Purged me of all sexual desire' is wonderfully formal for such a mundane cause. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Criss's ringtone: 'My ringtone is the sounds of cooking. Which is perfect, because I love cooking. But when I'm cooking...'
jokes.setup: Liz left 20 missed calls; Criss explains why he didn't hear them
jokes.punchline: His ringtone is sounds of cooking — which he can't hear when he's cooking — a circular design flaw he hasn't corrected because he loves cooking
jokes.explanation: Excellent character-specific absurdist logic. A cooking-sounds ringtone that's inaudible when cooking is a perfectly useless thing that Criss would choose and not think to change. The trailing '...But when I'm cooking...' as he realizes the flaw mid-sentence is great.

jokes.text: Jack: 'Lemon, please hang up. I can't listen to any more of this.'
jokes.setup: Criss has been explaining the cooking ringtone situation
jokes.punchline: Jack, still on the phone, loses patience with Criss's rambling explanation and demands Liz hang up
jokes.explanation: Good button on the cooking ringtone joke. Jack's exasperation is character-specific but the joke itself is fairly standard. Functional.

jokes.text: Liz: 'I stopped shopping at Kmart because I found out that Kathy Ireland didn't design any of her signature socks.'
jokes.setup: Liz admits she lets little things ruin stuff for her
jokes.punchline: Her example of a minor grievance she can't get over: Kathy Ireland's non-involvement in her own sock line at Kmart
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most quotable jokes. The specificity of 'Kathy Ireland's signature socks at Kmart' as the dealbreaker — and the implication that this is reasonable — is peak Liz Lemon. The joke works on multiple levels: it's a real brand/person (Kathy Ireland did have a Kmart line), the item (socks) is magnificently mundane, and Liz's moral outrage at celebrity non-involvement in their product line is perfectly specific to her character. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Criss reveals the table he built from 'fallen tree branches from Riverside Park' — where they first met — topped with a Herman Cain poster found in a dumpster.
jokes.setup: Liz asks where Criss got a table
jokes.punchline: He made it from park debris, and the tabletop is a discarded Herman Cain political poster — romantic sentiment meets absurd materials
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the episode's main table quest. The romantic sentiment (branches from where they met) + absurd material (Herman Cain poster from a dumpster) is perfectly Criss. Herman Cain specifically — a very timely 2012 political figure — as dumpster art is a nice period joke.

jokes.text: Liz: 'But how are we ever going to break up?' Criss: 'I don't know, maybe we never will. Maybe we'll still be celebrating Valentine's together 100 years from now.' Liz: 'Do you think our ape overlords will let us?'
jokes.setup: Criss is being romantically optimistic about their future
jokes.punchline: Liz's 'ape overlords' — she has a fully worked-out ape-ruled future dystopia as her baseline assumption
jokes.explanation: Classic Liz — her romantic optimism is immediately undercut by a Planet of the Apes future. The casual matter-of-fact 'ape overlords' as part of long-term planning is perfectly her. And Criss has a ready answer, suggesting he's accepted this worldview too.

jokes.text: The table Criss made: 'I gathered fallen tree branches from Riverside Park. That's where we first met.' / 'Yeah. And the top is a Herman Cain poster I found in a dumpster.'
jokes.setup: Liz is surprised to find a table — Criss somehow made one
jokes.punchline: The table is made from fallen branches and a Herman Cain campaign poster from a dumpster — the romantic gesture is undercut by the materials
jokes.explanation: A sweet joke — Criss found a creative solution using a Herman Cain poster (perfectly timely political reference, suggesting the poster was very recently dumpster-bound after his 2012 campaign failure) as a tabletop. The specificity of Herman Cain is inspired. 'Aw.' from Liz is the right response.

jokes.text: Hazel the page delivers a package to Liz's apartment, is amazed by Liz's life: 'You're the head writer of TGS? But you're so beautiful.' / 'Charlie what now?' / 'I love your brown hair. It's so bouncy, like the after picture in a lice ad.'
jokes.setup: Hazel arrives at Liz's apartment to deliver a package, discovers who Liz is
jokes.punchline: Her compliment is that Liz's hair looks like the 'after' picture in a lice treatment advertisement — presumably still not great hair, just better than 'before'
jokes.explanation: 'Like the after picture in a lice ad' is a wonderfully specific, perfectly backhanded compliment. The 'after' picture in a lice ad is still not glamorous hair — it's just lice-free. The specific reference (lice ad, bouncy, after picture) is exquisitely crafted. Deeply 30 Rock in its precision. Highly quotable and a genuine standout line. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Liz on her hair: 'Thank you. It's from intermittent washing.'
jokes.setup: Hazel has just complimented Liz's hair
jokes.punchline: Liz explains her bouncy hair results from infrequent washing — revealing poor hygiene as her beauty secret with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: 'It's from intermittent washing' is a perfect Liz Lemon line. Complete sincerity about poor hygiene as a hair care regimen, delivered without any self-consciousness. Maximum character integration and economy. Justifies 8.

jokes.text: Package delivery man to Liz: 'But you're so beautiful.' Then: 'I love your brown hair. It's so bouncy, like the "after" picture in a lice ad.'
jokes.setup: A delivery man is amazed that Liz is both the head writer of TGS and beautiful
jokes.punchline: His specific compliment: her hair is like the 'after' picture in a lice ad
jokes.explanation: The lice ad compliment is one of the episode's best jokes. It's a genuine compliment framed through the most unglamorous possible reference point — the 'after' picture in a lice treatment ad is actually meant to show healthy, shiny hair, but the comparison still implies the 'before' exists. The delivery man means it sincerely, which makes it funnier. Very quotable and original.

jokes.text: Hazel's reaction to Liz's apartment: 'Holy Moly, there's stairs? And a dining room table? Is this your boyfriend? He made me dinner? Mashed potatoes in a Martini glass. Who are you, the president? Of France?'
jokes.setup: Hazel discovers the details of Liz's life
jokes.punchline: Her amazement at seemingly mundane things (stairs, a table, homemade mashed potatoes) escalates to 'who are you, the president? Of France?' — treating basic middle-class comforts as presidential luxury
jokes.explanation: Good escalating reaction sequence. The mashed potatoes callback lands especially well because it pays off the earlier joke. 'Who are you, the president? Of France?' as the comedic peak is the right absurdist escalation — 'Of France?' adding the extra beat that elevates it.

jokes.text: Hazel: 'You are an inspiration, Liz Lemon. I am an inspiration.' Liz: 'I like her.' Hazel (leaving): 'I want your life. And I will have it.'
jokes.setup: Hazel is impressed by Liz's life
jokes.punchline: Hazel's 'I want your life' is followed by an ominous 'And I will have it' — immediately softened by Liz liking her
jokes.explanation: Great character button for Hazel's introduction arc. 'I will have it' as a sinister declaration of intent, paired with Liz completely missing the threat ('I like her'), is a perfect scene ending. Sets up future Hazel storylines ominously while being funny in the moment.

jokes.text: Jenna's pageant nightmare flashback: 'These shoes hurt, mommy.' Mother: 'Good. Focus on the pain, not on the fact that if you lose, I'm gonna pour acid on your Barbies.'
jokes.setup: Pete realizes Jenna needs pain to perform — she's always performed under duress
jokes.punchline: A flashback to Jenna's mother using Barbie acid threats as performance motivation — pure dark pageant mom horror
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark character backstory joke.
